lesson.title: Five Numbers, One Snapshot of a Distribution
lesson.summary: The five-number summary, minimum, Q1, median, Q3, and maximum, compresses an entire ordered data set into five landmark values that together describe center, spread, and range at a glance.
lesson.body:
A list of eighty, or eight hundred, individual data values is hard to hold in your head. The five-number summary solves that problem by reducing any quantitative data set to exactly five values: the minimum, the first quartile Q1, the median, the third quartile Q3, and the maximum. Reading those five numbers in order tells you, without ever seeing the raw list, roughly how the data is arranged from lowest to highest and where the bulk of it sits.

Each of the five numbers does a specific job. The minimum and maximum mark the full extent of the data and let you compute the range, found by subtracting the minimum from the maximum. The median marks the center. Q1 and Q3 mark the boundaries of the middle 50 percent of the data, and the distance between them, the interquartile range or IQR, measures how tightly or loosely that middle chunk is packed. Because Q1, the median, and Q3 are all resistant to outliers, meaning a single extreme value barely moves them, the five-number summary as a whole gives a sturdier picture of a distribution than the mean and standard deviation alone, especially when a data set is skewed or contains unusual values.

Return to the twelve quiz scores from before: 62, 65, 68, 70, 72, 75, 78, 80, 83, 85, 88, 92. The quartile work already done there gave a median of 76.5, Q1 of 69, and Q3 of 84. Reading off the sorted list directly, the minimum is 62 and the maximum is 92. So the five-number summary is: minimum 62, Q1 69, median 76.5, Q3 84, maximum 92. From those five numbers alone, the range is 92 minus 62, or 30 points, and the IQR is 84 minus 69, or 15 points. Notice that the range, which uses only the two most extreme scores, is twice as large as the IQR, which uses the middle half of the data. That gap is a clue that the lowest and highest scores are pulling the range wider than the typical spread of most students' scores would suggest.

The five-number summary is especially useful for comparing two or more groups side by side, since you can line up two sets of five numbers and immediately see which group scored higher on average, which group was more spread out, and whether one group had a wider gap between its lowest and typical scores. It is also the direct input for a boxplot, where each of the five numbers becomes a specific mark on the picture: the box edges at Q1 and Q3, the line inside the box at the median, and whiskers reaching out toward the minimum and maximum.

One caution worth remembering is that the five-number summary, on its own, cannot tell you the shape of the distribution with full precision. Two data sets can share an identical five-number summary while looking quite different in a histogram, if the data is packed unevenly between the landmark values. That is why the five-number summary is normally paired with a graph, most often a boxplot, rather than used as a complete replacement for looking at the data itself.
